description: Team Flammarion from AGH University of Krakow Space Technologies
summary:
FLAMMARION is an interactive Mars exploration and surface-mission operations platform that guides astronauts and mission planners from a global 3D planetary view down to live extravehicular activity (EVA) execution, demonstrated by a simulated mission in Jezero Crater.

We developed a seamless, three-stage spatial platform:

Area-to-Region Navigation: Continuous 3D zooming from global view to mission specific localization and high-resolution terrain mapping powered by NASA orbital imagery and elevation models.


Pre-Mission Planning: A trajectory planner and environmental timelapse simulator combining historical rover mission data; satellite imagery and Mars Orbital data with emulated power telemetry to generate a clear GO / NO-GO readiness assessment.


Intramission Monitoring: A dual-view real-time HUD (3D birds-eye flyover and first-person overlay) tracking astronaut life support, local Sol/GMT time, 30 cm-accuracy localization, and an autonomous scout drone flying 100–150 meters ahead. Powered by companion drone sensors and in-situ monitoring.


By pairing real scientific dataset; simulated data; and forecasting, with a Boolean-flag decision engine (PROCEED, HOLD, REROUTE, ABORT), FLAMMARION solves the challenge of planetary situational awareness—detecting weather changes, radiation spikes, and terrain hazards before they endanger human crews on Mars.
details:
Innovation

FLAMMARION is the first end-to-end application that simulates what a future crew would need to analyze before and during a surface expedition and extra-vehicular activity (EVA). Existing Mars visualization tools hold a retrospective and historic perspective - they show where the previous science rovers have been. In FLAMMARION every feature is visionary, yet grounded in research. The drone-ahead scouting concept is a crew-safety system inspired by Ingenuity’s proof of concept, but has yet to be demonstrated as a standard feature. With FLAMMARION, drone-ahead scouting will provide Astronauts with real-time data to assist in mission procedures and status. Additionally, every data telemetry number on screen carries a provenance tag so users always know whether they’re looking at a real measurement, a model output, or a simulation. 

Functionalities 

FLAMMARION is a web application that consists of three main stages of a crewed Mars surface mission. It is built to guide mission planners and astronauts through every phase to maximize the mission success.

Area-to-Region Navigation provides a realistic 3D Mars globe for broad-scale site analysis and mission planning. Users can explore the planet from a global view, select from USGS classified regions of the Martian surface, and choose IAU specified landmarks and regions of interest. As the user zooms from the global view down to selected mission (i.e. Jezero Crater), the display transitions into a high-resolution terrain map showing a planned exploration route, built from real NASA/USGS orbital imagery and elevation models.

The PRE-MISSION stage handles trajectory planning and readiness assessment while the crew is still in the habitat. An environmental time-lapse replays historical weather data from Curiosity (REMS) and Perseverance (MEDA), combined with emulated power telemetry, across the planned mission duration. This stage also displays a time-line of the mission; allows for the setting waypoints and science objectives; and provides the mission's elevation profile. The system then runs a “crew feedback” polling check to see if any predicted event is detected, and to check whether the environmental conditions fall within the threshold of the mission operation parameters to ensure Astronaut wellbeing and mission success. The system then outputs a clear GO / NO-GO decision on whether to proceed. 

If the mission is cleared, the app transitions to the Intra-Mission stage, whose primary objective is ensuring crew safety in real time. An autonomous scout drone flies 100–150 m ahead of the crew, scanning for terrain changes and hazardous dust devils, which can form within minutes, leaving the crew no time to evacuate, only to shelter. The system simultaneously tracks crew life-support vitals, local Sol and GMT time, and crew position with 30 cm localization accuracy.  A Boolean-flag decision engine continuously evaluates incoming telemetry and outputs one of four states: PROCEED, HOLD, REROUTE, or ABORT. This stage is implemented as a dual-view: real-time HUD with 3D bird’s-eye flyover; and first-person helmet overlay (as depicted with a toggle function within the application. This phase’s implementation is demonstrated as a time-step simulation with all data streaming in a continuous feed. The simulation, including timelapse control and anomalous condition injection commands, is accessible in the lower banner of the Mission page labelled “DEMO”. In future practice, real data from sensors, models, satellites, signal strength and drone-ahead data will be used when applied on an actual Mars mission. When the mission ends, the system generates a report with every step described. 

Data sources

Wherever possible, the team based its analysis on real historical data from NASA missions. Because not every system required for a crewed traverse exists yet, some data are realistically simulated. To maintain transparency, every value displayed in the application is tagged as HISTORIC, MODELLED, or SIMULATED. A full list of data sources and their provenance is accessible in the app under the “Data Sources” panel. 

Intended impact

The core problem FLAMMARION addresses is that no existing tool demonstrates an end-to-end workflow from planetary navigation to live EVA monitoring. By aggregating terrain exploration, environmental forecasting, and real-time situational awareness into one interface, the app gives astronauts and mission planners an integrated picture of what lies ahead, before and during a traverse. The drone-ahead architecture lets the system detect rapidly forming dust devils and new terrain obstacles, to maximize crew safety and mission success.

Tools and technologies

We built the application using CesiumJS with a custom Mars ellipsoid for 3D globe and terrain rendering, sourcing imagery tiles from the NASA Mars Trek WMTS API and processing a CTX GeoTIFF DEM offline into a static 40 m heightmap for Jezero Crater terrain. Simulation data streams are generated as timestamped NDJSON and replayed at configurable speed on the client side. Mars local solar time is computed using the Allison & McEwen (Mars24) algorithm. Real datasets include MEDA measurements from Jezero (air and ground temperature, pressure, wind speed, and UV), supplemented by Curiosity REMS data from Gale Crater as a labeled climatological reference. Surface imagery uses USGS CTX mosaics via Mars Trek (~6 m/px) and HiRISE imagery (25 cm/px) where available; modelled values such as solar flux and dust opacity are clearly tagged as MODELLED in the interface. For localization, the prototype uses a simulated position estimate with 30 cm accuracy. In a real implementation, this would fuse telemetry from multiple sources: visual odometry, inertial measurements, stereo depth mapping, and 360° camera cross-referencing against orbital imagery for precise triangulation, from both the crew and the scout drone, according to NASA state-of-the-art research. 

Languages

JavaScript (ES modules), Python 3, HTML/CSS, SVG, JSON / NDJSON / GeoJSON / JSON Schema, and GLSL (only inside CesiumJS).

App software

CesiumJS 1.135 (with @cesium/widgets 14.3.0), Vite 8, Node.js 22, npm, Ajv, and Node’s built-in test runner. No UI framework.

Data preparation (Python)

numpy, Pillow, tifffile, imagecodecs, pandas, rasterio, requests. 

Design and presentation

ChatGPT 6: mock-up visuals for the design reference

Figma: the presentation

AI development tools

Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5: app development and the presentation draft

Claude Code (cloud session): wrote and tested the code

Development, testing and hosting

Git and GitHub: version control and collaboration

Vercel: web-app hosting

Playwright with headless Chromium: automated click-throughs and screenshots

curl and openssl: probing data servers and certificates 

Factors the team considered

  1. Real Use Case Considerations: We wanted to consider all the important factors that would be beneficial to assist future Astronauts with navigation and safety on the Surface of Mars during vehicle expeditions and EVA. We considered what anomalous events might arise that would require future technological assistance. These included, but were not limited to: loss of communications signal, unmapped sub-surface ground features, anomalous weather formations (dust devils), solar-flare/coronal-mass-ejection alerts, electrostatic buildups, human life support (HLS) issues, solar flux coverage, as well as changes in the surface terrain that may have deviated from previous satellite imagery. We wanted to develop a system that could be used from the mission planning phase, all the way into the intermission phase. We wanted a platform that is both useful to mission control, the Martian base, and the Astronauts on the expedition. We considered implementing both a 3rd person perspective as well as an augmented reality (AR) style of informatics that could be displayed overlaid on as a heads-up display (HUD) on a future Astronaut’s visor.
  2. Geographic accuracy: all quadrangle boundaries, crater coordinates, and route distances use verified USGS/IAU data and geodesic calculations on the Mars reference ellipsoid
  3. Real unpredictable hazards: we didn't want to limit the demo to easily forecastable conditions and we focused on dust devils as the most acute, hard-to-predict threat to crew safety
  4. Forward compatibility with planned NASA missions: we identified which datasets future crewed missions will realistically produce, and simulated those we cannot yet access (SkyFall mission, launching 2028; future Mars positioning system (MPS) satellite constellations; etc)
  5. Jezero Crater as the mission site: chosen for its scientific importance, its relevance to active NASA operations, and the richness of available orbital and in-situ data
  6. Minimalist, mission-focused UI: surface information only when it aids decision-making, never overwhelm the user with too much detail and signal noise.
